title: AI-Based early warning and landslide Risk Monitoring System in NER
org: Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (MDoNER)
department: Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (MDoNER)
description:
Background:
The North Eastern Region (NER) frequently faces landslides, flash floods, road blockages, and slope failures due to heavy rainfall, fragile terrain, and unplanned hill cutting. These incidents often disrupt connectivity, damage infrastructure, delay emergency response, and isolate remote villages for days. Currently, monitoring of vulnerable zones is mostly reactive and dependent on manual reporting. There is limited use of real-time predictive systems for identifying high-risk zones and issuing early warnings to authorities and local communities. With increasing climate vulnerability in the region, there is a need for an AI-enabled real-time monitoring and prediction system that can help authorities take preventive action before disasters occur.
Description:
This problem statement proposes the development of an Al-powered early warning and monitoring platform capable of predicting and tracking landslide-prone areas in real time across the North Eastern Region. The solution should:
a. Collect and analyse data from: Rainfall patterns Soil moisture sensors Satellite imagery Terrain/slope data Historical landslide records b. Use AI/ML models to identify high-risk zones and predict possible landslide events.
c. Provide real-time alerts to district administrations, disaster management authorities, and local communities.
d. Integrate GIS mapping for visualization of vulnerable roads, villages, and infrastructure.
e. Allow citizens/field officials to upload geo-tagged photos/videos of cracks, slope movement or blocked roads.
f. Generate dashboards showing:
• Risk severity levels
• Road connectivity status
• Weather-linked risk forecasts
• Emergency response prioritisation. Support multilingual notifications and low-network/offline functionality for remote areas.
Expected Solution:
A scalable Al-based software platform with:
• Real-time GIS dashboard and risk heatmaps
• AI/ML-based predictive analytics engine
• Mobile/web application for field reporting and alerts.
• Integration with IMD weather APIs, satellite feeds, and sensor data
• Automated SMS/app-based early warning system
• Cloud-based architecture with offline sync support for remote regions The solution should improve disaster preparedness, reduce loss of life and infrastructure damage, and strengthen climate-resilient governance in the North Eastern Region.
summary: Innovation (5/5): draws on ai, ml, predictive applied to a disaster management problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (2/5): as a software build with higher integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (5/5): reaches a broad public/citizen base within Disaster Management. Tech Depth (5/5): centers on integration, sensor, gis. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (5/5): built to extend across states/users with modest rework. Total 25/30 -> Green verdict.

detail.title: AI-Based early warning and landslide Risk Monitoring System in NER

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a system that watches the hills in the North East for landslide warning signs, before they happen, and gets that warning to the people who need to act on it: district officers, disaster teams, and villagers on the ground.
overview.why_it_matters: NER's terrain and monsoon pattern make landslides a recurring event, not a rare one. Right now the region finds out a slope has failed after it's already blocked a road or buried something. A working prediction layer turns a reactive scramble into a planned evacuation.
pain_points: No standing real-time monitoring, most detection is a phone call after something has already moved.
Remote villages can be cut off for days after a slope failure, with no early signal to plan around.
Existing data (rainfall, soil, terrain, history) exists in separate places, nobody's fusing it into one risk picture.
overview.background: Heavy rainfall, unstable slopes, and hill-cutting for roads and construction combine to make NER landslide-prone. Monitoring today is manual and after-the-fact. MDoNER wants a predictive layer instead of a reactive one.
overview.whats_being_asked: An AI-powered platform that ingests rainfall, soil moisture, satellite imagery, terrain data, and historical landslide records, scores risk zones in real time, and pushes alerts to officials and residents before a slope fails.
expected_solution: AI/ML model that scores landslide risk per zone from the fused sensor + satellite + historical data.
Real-time alerting to district admin, disaster authorities, and local communities.
GIS map layer showing at-risk roads, villages, and infrastructure.
Citizen/field-officer upload channel for geo-tagged crack/slope-movement photos.
Dashboard: risk severity, road status, weather-linked forecast, response prioritisation.
Multilingual alerts and offline/low-network functionality for remote coverage.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough band. This isn't a single-model app, it's a live fusion of five different data streams (rainfall, soil, satellite, terrain, history) into one predictive score, with a citizen-reporting loop feeding back in. Most teams will only manage 2-3 of those streams in 36 hours; picking which ones and being upfront about it is the actual innovation move here.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. Count what's being asked: a prediction model, GIS visualization, multi-channel alerting, an upload/ingestion pipeline, and offline support, that's five separate subsystems, each non-trivial on its own.

competitive_landscape.note: Landslide/disaster-prediction PS types show up almost every SIH cycle, so evaluators have seen generic 'AI predicts disaster' pitches before. Differentiation has to come from the offline/low-network angle and the citizen-upload loop, those are the parts most teams skip.

innovation.note: Multi-source fusion (satellite + IoT + historical) for a live prediction score is genuinely non-trivial, not a wrapper.

invention.note: Five distinct technical subsystems asked for; a full build needs real system-design time, not just a weekend script.

technical_feasibility.note: Satellite imagery access and real historical landslide records are the two most likely to not be ready by hour 4, plan a synthetic fallback for both from the start.

impact_and_benefits.note: A missed warning here isn't an inconvenience, it's cut-off villages and possible casualties. Evaluators will weight this PS's impact heavily.

architecture.note: Sensor/satellite ingestion, an ML scoring layer, a GIS map, and a multilingual alert channel all have to talk to each other cleanly, that seam is where most demos will visibly break.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick if the team commits early to a reduced but real data pipeline rather than trying to wire up all five sources. The impact case is easy to defend, the technical bar is real but not unreasonable for 36 hours if scope is cut with intent.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: The Expected Solution section spells out six concrete deliverables, there's very little ambiguity about what a judge expects to see on stage.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Teams that try to build all five data integrations at once usually end up with none of them working reliably by hour 36. Pick two or three and make them solid.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Confirm before you start: can you actually get sample rainfall/soil/satellite data for NER, or will you be simulating it? Decide that in hour 0, not hour 20.

idea_0_4: Lock which 2-3 data sources you're actually integrating (recommend: rainfall + terrain slope data + historical records, satellite imagery is the hardest to source live).
Sketch the alert pipeline end to end on a whiteboard: input -> risk score -> map -> notification, before writing code.
Assign one person to own the ML scoring logic and one to own the GIS/map layer from hour 0, these can't be an afterthought.
prototype_4_22: Build the risk-scoring model against your chosen data sources, start with a rule-based or simple ML baseline, don't chase model accuracy over a working pipeline.
Get the GIS map rendering real risk zones, even with placeholder data, before building the alert layer on top of it.
Stand up the citizen-upload flow (photo + geotag) as a separate, simple module, it doesn't need to be smart, it needs to work.
integration_22_30: Wire the scoring output into the map and into the alert trigger, this is the seam most likely to break, budget real time for it.
Test the offline/low-network path specifically, this is called out explicitly in the official text and evaluators will ask about it.
Run the whole pipeline against a messy input (missing sensor reading, delayed data) not just the clean demo case.
polish_30_36: Build the dashboard view: risk severity, road status, forecast, prioritisation, in that visual order.
Rehearse a tight walkthrough: the NER problem, your data pipeline, the live map, then the alert in action.
Prepare a direct answer for 'what happens when your satellite/sensor data isn't available', because it will be asked.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Don't demo the happy path. Kill the network mid-demo and show the offline alert still queues and fires when connectivity returns, that's the one feature every competing team will have skipped.

strengths: Deliverables are explicit in the official text, less time lost interpreting scope.
Genuine technical substance across ML, GIS, and alerting, not a thin UI over a database.
weaknesses: High invention effort stacked on real data-sourcing risk, plan to cut scope on purpose, early.
Multiple subsystems touching each other means integration risk is real, don't leave it to the last few hours.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: 2 technical-heavy (ML + backend), 1 frontend/GIS, 1 flex for integration and demo prep.
team_fit.approach: Spend the first hour deciding your real data sources before assigning any code work, the team split only makes sense once that's locked.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: A baseline risk-scoring function, a map UI shell, and boilerplate alert-sending code, all standard patterns an AI tool can scaffold quickly.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Deciding which data sources are trustworthy enough to score risk from, tuning the model against real (or realistically synthetic) landslide history, and the offline-sync logic, that's domain judgment, not boilerplate.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-scaffolded demo that's never been tested against a dropped connection or a missing sensor reading will fall over the moment a judge asks 'what if this data isn't available', which they will.

data_resource_availability.status: Historical landslide records and live satellite imagery for NER are not trivially available to a hackathon team in 36 hours, this is the single biggest sourcing risk in the PS.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: Use publicly available rainfall data (IMD) as your real source, and construct a synthetic but realistic terrain/historical dataset for the rest, be upfront about which parts are synthetic in your demo, judges respect honesty here more than a faked 'real' dataset.

judge_qna.question: What happens to your risk score if the satellite imagery feed is down?
judge_qna.strong_answer: The model falls back to the rainfall + terrain + historical layers alone, at lower confidence, and the dashboard flags the reduced-confidence state rather than silently showing a false-precision number.
judge_qna.follow_up: How do you communicate 'lower confidence' to a district officer who needs to make a decision right now?

judge_qna.question: How do you validate that your model's risk zones are actually accurate, not just plausible-looking?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Back-test against known historical landslide events in the region, if the model would have flagged those zones as high-risk beforehand, that's your validation, not accuracy on synthetic data alone.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's your false-positive rate, and what does an unnecessary evacuation alert cost?

judge_qna.question: Why should a district administration trust an AI alert over their existing manual process?
judge_qna.strong_answer: It's not a replacement, it's a earlier signal, the manual process still confirms before acting, the system just moves the first alert from 'after the road is blocked' to 'before the slope fully fails'.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's your false-negative cost if the model misses a real event?
